title: Sync extension manifest
description: What a package says about itself. Four things read this file — the packer, the registry's CI, Sync's Rust loader and the window — and this is what validates it for all of them. Sync's reader is the authority: where the two disagree, the reader is right and this is behind.

manifestVersion.description: The format this file is written in. Read before anything else, so a package from the future is told it needs a newer Sync rather than being told a field name is unknown — which would be true and useless.

id.description: Permanent, and the namespace every kind it publishes is prefixed with. Nothing that could be a path: an id with a slash in it escapes the artefact directory.

version.description: The package's own version, which is neither the API's nor the application's.

summary.description: One line, in the catalogue's voice: what a project gains by adding it.

description.description: What it is, at the length a decision to install one deserves.

icon.description: The mark shown for this package, as a lucide-react icon name in that library's own kebab-case spelling — "book-marked", "circle-dot", "folder-git-2". Any name at https://lucide.dev/icons is one the host can draw; a name outside it is drawn with the neutral mark, and `sync-ext check` reports it. It is a name and not a file so that it still resolves once the package has been removed, which is what a record written by this package needs.

syncApi.description: A semver range over the host's SYNC_API_VERSION, such as ^2.0. Checked before a line of the package is executed.

capabilities.description: Named things the build must be able to do. A capability the host has never heard of is a refusal, not a warning: it arrives in exactly one situation — a package built against a newer host — and treating it as satisfied would run an extension that asked for something and did not get it.

net.description: Where it may reach, and the whole of what it may reach. The list is the permission: a request to anything else is refused in Rust before it leaves the machine, on the first request and on every redirect after it. Each entry is exactly one host — no scheme, no port, no path and no wildcard, because a pattern is a family of hosts nobody enumerated.

hosts.description: Host names, as a URL spells them.

secrets.description: Secrets the host writes into a header for you, so your code never holds one. Each entry names one of your own keychain entries and one host from the list above; Sync reads the value in Rust and puts it in the header. This is the recommended way to use a credential — the other way, reading the value yourself, needs the `vault` capability and exists for what a header cannot carry, such as a signature.

host.description: Which of `net.hosts` it goes to, and only that one. A token for one API arriving at another is how a credential reaches somebody who never asked for it, so a package talking to two writes two entries.

header.description: The header the value is written into — `authorization` for almost everything, and an API key often wants `x-api-key`.

secret.description: What you call it in your own corner of the keychain. The name only: the owner half is your package's id and is composed in Rust, so this cannot name anybody else's entry.

scheme.description: What goes in front of the value — `Bearer` for most. Absent writes the value alone, which is what an API-key header wants. A scheme rather than a template: `Bearer {}` would be a small language in a manifest, and every one of those grows.

requires.description: What it needs from the project rather than from the build.

areas.description: The sections it contributes to the window. An extension is not necessarily a screen, and declaring none is an ordinary answer.

id.description: Unique within the extension. The window addresses it as <extension>/<id>.

description.description: What the section is for, where a column needs explaining.

frame.description: One of the shapes the shell draws, and the module must fill exactly that frame's columns: browse has a navigator and an inspector, list a navigator, detail an inspector, single neither. Returning a column the frame does not have fails to install rather than being dropped.

icon.description: The mark on this section's row, as a lucide-react icon name — the same vocabulary as the package's own icon.

badge.description: A count the host draws on this section's row. Nothing of the package runs to produce it, which is the point: a section is mounted the first time it is visited, so a number only a mounted section could raise would be missing on the first launch after a project is opened — exactly when somebody wants it. Omit it for a section with nothing to count.

kinds.description: Which kinds are counted, and omitting it counts every kind this section opens — the ordinary answer, because the manifest has already said which those are. Name them only where one extension has two sections over one vocabulary. Each is prefixed with the extension id, by the rule opens.kinds reads: a badge over another extension's records is a number nobody can act on.

freshness.description: Which of the states the engine derives are counted, and omitting it counts every state.

types.description: Paths inside the package, each one type definition. Every kind they publish is prefixed with the extension's id and a dot: two extensions may both want to call something a decision, and neither may redefine the other's.

opens.description: Which records this extension knows how to show. Publishing a type and opening one are two contributions, not one.

kinds.description: Kinds it opens, which are normally the kinds it publishes. A kind belonging to another extension is refused.

projectTypes.description: Whether it opens the types the project made itself. Exactly one installed extension should claim it; the host prefers whichever the project declares.

prompt.description: Path to what a connected agent is told, as prose. Written into the project on install, because the agent reads it through a server that has never seen the catalogue.

dependencies.description: What it needs fetched before it works well.

npm.description: Packages from npm, by name. What the host fetches is the adapter set it knows how to fetch — installing an arbitrary package on an extension's say-so is a much larger permission than the one being asked for.

ui.description: The built ES module, relative to the package root. Optional, because an extension that publishes only a vocabulary and a prompt has no code to run — and required the moment it declares a section, because a section is drawn by code.

styles.description: The built stylesheet, relative to the package root. The host adds it to the document when it loads the module and takes it away with it. Optional, and only meaningful beside `ui`: it holds the utility rules this package's own markup uses, which the window's stylesheet does not contain — Tailwind generates only what it finds in the window's own source, and a package is not in it. It carries no values: every colour and step in it is a `var()` the window defines, so retinting the window retints the package.

service.description: The built service module, relative to the package root: where this package's handlers live, for what it does when no screen is mounted. Optional, and independent of `ui` — a package may have a screen and no handlers, or handlers and no screen. It is read by the host in Rust and never served to the window, so a handler is not code any document can reach.

lifecycle.description: Handlers called because something happened to the package itself, rather than because a clock struck or another extension asked. Each value is the name of a handler the service module returns.

installed.description: Called once, when this package is installed into a project. It is synchronous and has a person in front of it, so a handler that fails here fails the install and says why.

schedule.description: Handlers called because a clock struck. Interval rather than cron: a syntax that can say `at 03:00 on weekdays` buys a timezone question and a missed-while-asleep question, and nothing here needs either. Lateness is not made up for — a machine asleep for six hours runs a handler once when it wakes, not six times.

description.description: What this handler does, in your own words, for the page somebody decides from. Required, because the handler's own name is not shown and `every` says only how often: without this the page can say `runs every 6h` and not what it runs. The host writes the cadence beside your sentence and never takes it from here, so the two cannot disagree.
description.$comment: Whitespace is not a sentence, and the host refuses one. A check that accepts what the host will refuse is the failure this repository already paid for once, in the other direction.

tools.description: Handlers an agent may call, and everything it is told before deciding to. The third occasion, and the first whose caller is not the application: a clock and an install happen here, and a tool is a name somebody else says. An agent reaches one as `<your id>.<tool>`, through Sync's own `sync_call`, and reads what each takes from `sync_instructions`.

name.description: What an agent calls it, without your id in front. Lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, starting with a letter — a dot would read as the separator between your id and this. Separate from `handler` because the two are named for different readers: one is your own name for a function, the other is a fragment an agent puts in a call.

description.description: What the tool does, in your own words. Required, and it is the whole of what an agent decides on: a tool with no sentence is one nothing will ever call correctly.
description.$comment: Whitespace is not a sentence, and the host refuses one.

input.description: The shape of what it takes, as JSON Schema, carried whole. Sync never reads what an argument means — that is yours — but it does check arguments against this before your handler runs, and refuses in words naming what was wrong. Absent is a tool that takes nothing.

allOf.$comment: A section with nothing to draw it is refused rather than shipped as an empty column.
A stylesheet with no module to style is a file nobody asked for: styles are the markup's, and the markup is in the module.
An occasion with nothing to call is an intention rather than a capability, and the install would be the first thing to find out.

Running code with no screen is something a person agrees to before the package is installed, and the card is where they agree to it. A package that ships handlers and asks for nothing would be running code that was never on the card.
The same rule as for `lifecycle`, one occasion over: a package that says when to call a handler and ships nothing to call it in has declared an intention rather than a capability.

A second capability rather than a wider reading of the first. `background` is agreeing that this package runs code; `schedule` is agreeing that it runs it while nobody is there. A person shown only the first agreed to the narrower of two different things.

The same rule as `background`, one permission over: reading something nobody in this window wrote is something a person agrees to before the package is installed, and the card is where they agree to it.

And the direction the other capabilities cannot be wrong in. A service module is in the package whether or not it was declared, so `background` can only be missing; a host list is the permission itself, so a package can also ask for the network and name nowhere to reach — a permission with no extent, and an agreement somebody made for nothing.

handlerName.description: The name of a handler the service module returns. Not prefixed with the extension id, unlike a kind: a kind goes into a corpus everybody shares, while a handler's name is only ever read beside the package that declared it.

interval.description: How often a handler runs: a count and a unit, like `30m`, `6h` or `1d`. Minutes, hours or days, and deliberately no seconds — the unit set is the floor, so the shortest interval anybody can express is one minute and there is no separate minimum to state and then disagree with. A leading zero is refused rather than normalised, so `1h` has one spelling.

insidePath.description: A path that stays inside the package: relative, no backslashes, no segment that is empty, `.` or `..`. A path that climbs reads a file the archive does not contain.
